rows.symptom: The overnight order-import job is supposed to guarantee that a bad line can never undo work already done, but it isn't holding up: when a batch import run hits a bad line partway through (say line 3 of 4, with a blank Customer No. or a zero/negative Quantity) and errors out, none of the earlier lines in that run show up as Imported Orders either, and their Status is back to Pending as if ImportBatch never touched them. The same thing happens if the failure is a duplicate-key crash while writing an Imported Order instead of a guard error. Rerunning the batch after fixing the bad line then re-imports everything from line 1, including lines that (per the log) were supposedly already processed on the failed run. Nothing about the code looks wrong on a read-through, and every clean batch (no poison line) imports perfectly and only once.
rows.groundTruth: Mechanism: in ImportBatch (codeunit "Order Import Batch"), the repeat/until loop over pending Order Import Lines correctly guards each line (TestField("Customer No."), Quantity <= 0 check), inserts its Imported Order row, and flips Status to Imported inside the loop — but the Commit() call that should follow each line's successful write was moved to run exactly once, after the loop exits, instead of once per iteration inside the loop body. Why the symptom follows: AL keeps one open write transaction per session until it is either explicitly made permanent with Commit() or the whole transaction rolls back on an unhandled error. With no per-line Commit(), every line's Insert()/Modify() in a given ImportBatch call remains part of the same still-open transaction. When a later line raises an error (TestField failure, the Error() call, or an insert-time duplicate-key exception), AL's default error handling rolls back everything written since the last transaction boundary — which, with the commit moved out of the loop, is everything the entire run did, including the lines that were fully valid and processed before the poison line. The loop never reaches its own Commit() call (it sits after `until`), so nothing from a failing run is ever made durable, and a rerun sees all of that batch's lines still Pending and reprocesses them from scratch, producing the "already-imported lines lost, then re-imported as if new" behavior. It is invisible in any all-success batch because the single end-of-loop Commit() still fires once the loop finishes cleanly, matching the happy-path test exactly. The fix: move Commit() back inside the repeat/until loop, immediately after OrderImportLine.Modify() (i.e., after each line's Imported Order insert and Status flip), so every successfully imported line becomes a separate, already-committed transaction before the loop advances to the next line — that way a later error can only unwind the currently-in-flight line, never the ones already committed.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified the exact planted defect: the single Commit() sitting after the repeat/until loop in codeunit "Order Import Batch".ImportBatch, so any later line's error (TestField, explicit Error(), or duplicate-key on Insert) rolls back the entire still-open transaction including earlier lines' Insert("Imported Order") and Status flips, which is precisely the ground-truth mechanism including why the rerun re-imports everything (Status genuinely reverted to Pending in the database). The proposed fix moves Commit() inside the loop immediately after OrderImportLine.Modify(), matching the ground-truth fix exactly, making each line durable before the next iterates so a poison line only unwinds its own in-flight work. Clean-batch behavior is preserved (each line still commits once), so no other behavior breaks.

rows.symptom: Credit control set up per-customer order caps ("Max Order Amount (LCY)") so sales users can't release an order above the agreed ceiling, but the cap simply isn't working: users are releasing orders that are well over their customer's limit and the order goes straight to Released with no error at all. It doesn't seem to matter how large the order is or how small the cap is set - nothing ever blocks. Orders for customers with no cap configured (cap left at 0) release fine, as expected, but so does everything else - the cap effectively has zero effect on any order, however far over the limit it is.
rows.groundTruth: Mechanism: in codeunit "Order Cap Enforcement" (OrderCapEnforcement.Codeunit.al), the subscriber EnforceOrderCapOnBeforeReleaseSalesDoc (bound to Codeunit "Release Sales Document", event OnBeforeReleaseSalesDoc) never calls SalesHeader.CalcFields(Amount) before evaluating `if SalesHeader.Amount > Customer."Max Order Amount (LCY)"`. Sales Header's Amount field is a FlowField (SumIndexField sourced from Sales Line, sum of line amounts excluding VAT); on a Record variable that was not populated via CalcFields, an unrequested FlowField reads as its default value (0 for a Decimal), not the true computed sum. Since a real order amount is virtually never <= 0, `Amount > Cap` is essentially always false, so the Error() branch is never reached and the release routine proceeds unobstructed for every order regardless of actual amount or cap size. All the surrounding logic is otherwise correct: document-type filtering (Order only), sell-to customer lookup, and the zero-means-no-cap short-circuit all behave as specified - only the amount comparison is silently defeated. The correct fix is to insert `SalesHeader.CalcFields(Amount);` immediately before the comparison (as in the original working solution), which forces BC to compute the FlowField from the Sales Line records so SalesHeader.Amount reflects the true line-amount sum before it's compared to the cap. A judge should credit any diagnosis that identifies: (1) the Amount field is a FlowField that requires CalcFields to populate, (2) it is read directly without a preceding CalcFields call in this subscriber, and (3) the observable effect is that Amount defaults to 0 so the over-cap comparison is always false, letting every order release unconditionally. A diagnosis that says "the cap check never fires" without identifying the missing CalcFields/FlowField mechanism, or that blames the wrong condition (e.g. the zero-cap exit, the document-type check, or the customer lookup), should not be credited as correct.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified the exact planted mechanism: Sales Header "Amount" is a FlowField that is never populated without CalcFields, the subscriber EnforceOrderCapOnBeforeReleaseSalesDoc in codeunit "Order Cap Enforcement" reads it directly so it evaluates as 0, making `Amount > Cap` false for every order and letting all releases through - matching all three elements the ground truth requires (FlowField needs CalcFields, no CalcFields call in this subscriber, Amount defaults to 0 so the comparison never trips). The proposed fix inserts `SalesHeader.CalcFields(Amount);` immediately before the comparison, identical to the reference fix, and leaves the document-type filter, customer lookup, zero-cap exit, and error text untouched, so it cures the symptom without side effects. The solver also correctly noted the zero-cap early exit is an unrelated, correct guard rather than the culprit.

rows.symptom: Customers are getting free shipping on large orders even though nobody in the org has turned the "Q3 large-order incentive" campaign on. Any order of 1000 or more processed through CalculateFreight comes back with a freight charge of 0, system-wide, all the time — not just when a specific process explicitly enables the promotion. The default 10%-of-order freight calculation never runs for qualifying amounts, and there is no code path anywhere that toggles this behavior on or off; it is simply always active for every caller.
rows.groundTruth: Defect: codeunit "Free Freight Promotion" (70201) subscribes to the "Freight Charge Calculator" (70200) integration event OnBeforeCalculateFreight via [EventSubscriber(...)], but the codeunit is missing the property `EventSubscriberInstance = Manual;`. In AL, a codeunit's default EventSubscriberInstance is Static, which means the platform automatically instantiates the subscriber codeunit and wires its event subscriber methods to fire for every invocation of the published event, for every caller, session-wide, with no explicit registration required. The correct design (per the task spec) requires the promotion to be opt-in: it must only fire while some caller has explicitly executed BindSubscription against an instance of this codeunit, and must NOT fire otherwise (e.g. CalculateFreight(5000) called with nobody having bound the promotion must still return the default 500.00, not 0). Because EventSubscriberInstance is left at its default (Static) instead of being set to Manual, GrantFreeFreightOnLargeOrders unconditionally fires for every call to CalculateFreight where Amount >= 1000, setting Freight := 0 and IsHandled := true and short-circuiting the default Round(Amount * 0.1, 0.01) calculation — regardless of whether BindSubscription was ever called. This is the exact inverse of the intended behavior: it should be silent-by-default and active-only-when-bound, but instead it is active-by-default and cannot be turned off via unbinding (Static subscribers ignore BindSubscription/UnbindSubscription entirely). The symptom (free freight for large orders "for everyone, always") follows directly: the discriminating test is calling CalculateFreight with Amount >= 1000 WITHOUT binding the promotion codeunit — a correct implementation returns the default 10% charge in that case, while this buggy version returns 0. The fix is to add `EventSubscriberInstance = Manual;` as a codeunit property on "Free Freight Promotion", which suppresses automatic static instancing so the subscriber method only executes on an instance obtained via BindSubscription, and stops executing once that instance is unbound (or the session holding it ends). A judge should credit any diagnosis that correctly identifies: (a) the subscriber fires unconditionally / for every caller instead of only when explicitly bound, and (b) the root cause is the absence of manual/opt-in event subscriber instancing (missing EventSubscriberInstance = Manual, or equivalent phrasing about static vs. manual subscriber binding) — partial credit for identifying only the symptom (unconditional firing) without naming the specific property/mechanism.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver correctly located the defect (codeunit 70201's EventSubscriber on OnBeforeCalculateFreight firing unconditionally for every caller) but missed the actual root cause: the missing `EventSubscriberInstance = Manual;` property. Worse, it affirmatively denied the mechanism exists ("subscription is not something that can be 'installed but dormant'"), which is exactly what Manual instancing plus BindSubscription provides in AL. Its fix (a PromotionEnabled boolean with a setter, keeping the subscriber static) would suppress the symptom but cannot restore the intended opt-in behavior: with default static instancing the platform fires the subscriber on its own instance, so a caller's SetPromotionEnabled(true) on a local codeunit variable never reaches the firing instance, and BindSubscription (the spec-required activation path) still would not work — leaving the promotion permanently dead. Per the ground truth's own rubric this is the partial-credit case: unconditional firing identified without naming the static-vs-manual instancing mechanism, plus a fix that does not fully work.
rows.fableWhy: The solver's diagnosis matches the ground truth on both required elements: (a) it identifies that the subscriber in codeunit 70201 fires unconditionally for every raise of OnBeforeCalculateFreight in every session, and (b) it names the exact mechanic — the missing EventSubscriberInstance property defaulting to Static automatic binding instead of Manual opt-in via BindSubscription. The proposed fix adds `EventSubscriberInstance = Manual;` to "Free Freight Promotion" while leaving the calculator, event signature, and threshold logic untouched, which is precisely the ground-truth fix and restores the default 10% freight for unbound callers while preserving the promotion when a process explicitly binds. The solver also correctly traces the short-circuit path (IsHandled := true skipping the Round(Amount * 0.1, 0.01) default), so there is no mechanic mismatch anywhere.

rows.symptom: The nightly legacy-amount import job (codeunit "Legacy Amount Import Job", procedure ImportBatch calling "Legacy Amount Import".ImportLine) always reports zero lines imported, even when every single line in the batch is a perfectly well-formatted, non-negative amount. Nothing ever lands in the "Legacy Amount Entry" table, there is no error message anywhere, and ImportLine simply returns false for every entry code no matter what amount text is passed in. Directly calling ParseAmount or TryParseAmount with the same amount texts works fine and returns the correct values, which makes the empty table even more confusing to whoever is investigating.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: codeunit 70001 "Legacy Amount Import", local procedure DoImportLine (decorated [TryFunction]), called from the public ImportLine.

Mechanic: DoImportLine both parses the amount (Amount := ParseAmount(AmountText)) AND performs the database write (LegacyAmountEntry.Insert(true)) inside the body of a procedure marked [TryFunction]. Business Central blocks database write operations (Insert/Modify/Delete) executed inside a [TryFunction]-decorated procedure by default (the DisableWriteInsideTryFunctions platform behavior) — the write throws a runtime error the instant it executes. Because DoImportLine is itself a TryFunction, that thrown error is caught by the try-function machinery exactly like any other runtime error would be, and DoImportLine simply returns false to its caller instead of propagating the error. It does not matter whether AmountText was valid or invalid, or whether Amount parsed correctly first — the moment execution reaches the Insert() call, it fails and DoImportLine returns false.

Why the symptom follows: ImportLine's return value is exit(DoImportLine(...)), so ImportLine inherits this always-false behavior unconditionally. ImportBatch counts only calls where ImportLine returns true, so ImportedCount is always 0 and "Legacy Amount Entry" never receives a row, for any input. ParseAmount and TryParseAmount (via the separate, write-free local procedure DoParseAmount) are structurally unaffected because they never touch the database, which is why calling them directly still works correctly and isolates the fault to the write path specifically, not the parsing logic.

Correct fix: remove the Insert() call from inside the [TryFunction]-decorated procedure. DoImportLine (or a helper it calls) must only parse the amount inside the try scope; ImportLine must check that Boolean result first, and only after it returns true, perform LegacyAmountEntry."Entry Code" := EntryCode; LegacyAmountEntry.Amount := Amount; LegacyAmountEntry.Insert(true); as ordinary statements in ImportLine itself (outside any TryFunction body) — mirroring how DoParseAmount/TryParseAmount already keep parsing separate from persistence. A grading test should seed several valid amount texts, call ImportLine, and assert both that it returns true and that "Legacy Amount Entry" actually contains the row with the correct Amount — the pre-fix code passes a "returns false, no error" check but fails a "row actually got inserted" check.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified the exact planted defect: codeunit "Legacy Amount Import", local [TryFunction] procedure DoImportLine performing LegacyAmountEntry.Insert(true) inside the try scope, which the DisableWriteInsideTryFunctions platform restriction fails at runtime regardless of input, leaving ImportLine false and the table empty while the write-free ParseAmount/TryParseAmount path stays healthy. Its fix mirrors the ground-truth prescription almost verbatim (parse via the existing TryParseAmount inside the try scope, then perform the field assignments and Insert as ordinary statements in ImportLine, deleting DoImportLine), so it would cure the symptom without altering other behavior. The one mismatch is a subsidiary propagation detail: the solver claims the NavNclTryFunctionWriteException escapes the try boundary uncaught, whereas ground truth says the try machinery catches it and returns false; this does not change the identified object, the operative mechanic (blocked write inside a TryFunction failing at the Insert for every input), or the correctness of the remedy.

rows.symptom: In the price-list import review tool, an item's price lines that include an open-ended entry (no "Ending Date" set, meaning it stays valid indefinitely) almost never get flagged as overlapping anything else, even when the coverage summary clearly shows another line's window sitting entirely inside that open-ended line's date range. The tool reports "no overlapping price lines" or an undercounted conflict total for items that obviously have colliding validity windows once an open-ended line is involved, while items whose lines all have concrete start and end dates are counted correctly. The continuous-coverage merge view itself (which periods the item is priced under, and when) still looks correct — only the "how many pairs collide" count is wrong.
rows.groundTruth: Defect is in local procedure PeriodsOverlap inside codeunit 70001 "CG Price Validity Analyzer" (used by CountConflictingPairs, NOT by MergeValidityPeriods - the merge/coverage logic is untouched and correct). Correct semantics: exit(((EndA = 0D) or (StartB <= EndA)) and ((EndB = 0D) or (StartA <= EndB))) - i.e. "A and B overlap if (A never ends, or B starts at/before A's end) AND (B never ends, or A starts at/before B's end)". The planted bug flips the first clause's `or` to `and`: exit(((EndA = 0D) and (StartB <= EndA)) and ((EndB = 0D) or (StartA <= EndB))). Mechanism: 0D (blank date) sorts as the lowest possible date in AL comparisons. When EndA = 0D (line A is open-ended / never expires), the buggy clause now additionally requires StartB <= EndA, i.e. StartB <= 0D - which is true only when B's own Starting Date is also blank. So whenever line A is open-ended and line B has any real (non-blank) starting date, the AND short-circuits to false regardless of whether the two periods actually overlap in time, and CountConflictingPairs silently drops that pair from the count. Symmetric case (EndB=0D, StartA blank) is unaffected because only the FIRST `or` was flipped, not the second - so the bug is asymmetric: it suppresses matches on the "A" side of the pairwise comparison whenever A is the open-ended line, for any B with a concrete start date. Two ordinary date-bounded lines (no 0D ends) are unaffected since EndA=0D is false for both terms, leaving the AND redundant-but-harmless (StartB<=EndA still gates correctly as it's the same test in both branches when EndA<>0). A correct fix restores the `or` in the first clause (making both open-ended checks disjunctive with the corresponding start/end comparison, matching the second clause's already-correct `or`) or equivalently rewrites PeriodsOverlap as a single symmetric expression that treats a blank Ending Date as "infinitely far in the future" (e.g., substitute a very-late sentinel date for 0D before comparing) rather than leaving 0D's low-sort-order to interact with an `and`. Diagnosis credit requires identifying that the count is wrong (not the merge/coverage output), that only open-ended (blank Ending Date) lines are involved, and that the mechanism is the boolean-operator error inside PeriodsOverlap's overlap test - not e.g. a SetFilter/key issue, not the ValidateLines error path, and not something in EmitPeriod or the merge loop.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified the exact planted defect: the first clause of PeriodsOverlap in codeunit 70001 uses `and` where `or` belongs, matching ground truth's object, procedure, and mechanic precisely, including the key 0D-sorts-lowest mechanism (the flipped clause collapses to `StartB <= 0D`, satisfiable only when B's start is also blank, so open-ended-A pairs are silently dropped from CountConflictingPairs). It also correctly explained why MergeValidityPeriods is unaffected (it has its own independent sweep-line test and never calls PeriodsOverlap), satisfying all three diagnosis-credit requirements. The proposed fix is character-for-character the ground truth's correct expression: exit(((EndA = 0D) or (StartB <= EndA)) and ((EndB = 0D) or (StartA <= EndB))), which cures the symptom without touching merge/coverage or concrete-vs-concrete behavior. The only blemish is a slightly hand-wavy sentence about why fully-dated pairs still count correctly, but that matches ground truth's own characterization and does not affect the mechanic or the fix.

rows.symptom: Running the monthly royalty statement for an agreement a second time in the same session (or generating statements for several agreements back-to-back reusing the same total variables) produces totals that are too high — TotalAmount and TotalCredits keep climbing across runs instead of reflecting only the current agreement's performances. The individual statement lines themselves look correct (right plays, right per-line Amount and Credits, right order), but the two summary figures at the bottom of the statement are inflated by whatever was left over from the previous statement that was built. A fresh agreement with zero performances still reports the leftover totals from the last agreement processed instead of showing 0.00 and 0.
rows.groundTruth: Defect location: codeunit "Royalty Statement", procedure BuildStatement (object id 70102). At the top of the procedure, the buffer is cleared correctly (RoyaltyStatementLine.Reset(); RoyaltyStatementLine.DeleteAll();) but the two accumulator var parameters are never initialized to zero before the loop — the lines `TotalAmount := 0;` and `TotalCredits := 0;` that must appear immediately after the buffer clear are missing entirely. The loop body only ever does `TotalAmount += RoyaltyStatementLine.Amount;` / `TotalCredits += RoyaltyStatementLine.Credits;`, which accumulate onto whatever value the caller's TotalAmount/TotalCredits var parameters already held on entry. Because these are `var` parameters, any caller that passes in variables already holding a value (either because it pre-set them, or because it is reusing the same TotalAmount/TotalCredits variables across two consecutive BuildStatement calls for different agreements) gets a result silently added on top of that stale value instead of a clean recomputation. This does not affect LineAmount or LineCredits (both are pure functions of Category/Audience and are correct), does not affect which performances are selected (the SetRange("Agreement No., ...) filter is correct), does not affect line count/order/Line No. numbering (correct, 1..N in Entry No. order), and does not affect per-line Amount/Credits values written into RoyaltyStatementLine (correct). It also does not affect the buffer itself, which IS properly cleared via DeleteAll() — only the two scalar total accumulators leak stale/pre-set values. An agreement with zero matching performances is the sharpest manifestation: BuildStatement exits after FindSet() returns false, having cleared the buffer but never touched TotalAmount/TotalCredits, so whatever the caller passed in comes back unchanged instead of 0/0. The correct fix is to add `TotalAmount := 0; TotalCredits := 0;` right after the buffer clear (RoyaltyStatementLine.Reset(); RoyaltyStatementLine.DeleteAll();) and before the SetRange/FindSet block, so every call starts both totals from a clean zero regardless of what the caller passed in or what a prior call left behind. A diagnosis is correct if it identifies that BuildStatement fails to reset/initialize TotalAmount and TotalCredits (the two var accumulator parameters) before summing, as distinct from any claim about the buffer not being cleared, the record filter being wrong, the per-line fee/credit formulas being wrong, or line ordering/numbering being wrong — all of which are correct in this code.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified exactly the planted defect: codeunit 70102 "Royalty Statement", procedure BuildStatement, where the var accumulator parameters TotalAmount/TotalCredits are only ever incremented with += and never initialized to zero, while correctly noting the RoyaltyStatementLine buffer IS properly cleared (matching ground truth's exclusions). It also correctly explained the sharpest manifestation, the zero-performance agreement exiting at FindSet() with the caller's stale values untouched. The proposed fix adds `TotalAmount := 0; TotalCredits := 0;` immediately after the Reset()/DeleteAll() and before the SetRange/FindSet block, exactly as ground truth prescribes, with no other behavioral changes to line building, ordering, or per-line amounts.

rows.symptom: When we run Allocate Charge on an invoice, the individual line amounts on the Invoice Charge Line records don't add up to the Total Charge Amount on the header. Sometimes we're a cent short, sometimes there's a stray extra cent nobody's line accounts for. It's worst on invoices where several lines have equal weight and the fair share works out to a half-cent each — a 0.99 handling fee split across six equal-weight lines comes back totaling 1.02 instead of 0.99, and a plain three-way split of a 100.00 charge only adds up to 99.99. Finance can't post these batches because the charge lines never close exactly to the total.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: codeunit 70102 "Invoice Charge Alloc. Mgt.", procedure AllocateCharge, in the second loop over ChargeLine. The line `LineAmount := Round(ChargeHeader."Total Charge Amount" * ChargeLine.Weight / WeightSum, 0.01)` computes and rounds each line's exact proportional share independently, with no tracking of a running/cumulative total and no correction step afterward. Each line's exact share (TotalAmount * Weight / WeightSum) is rounded to the nearest cent in isolation, so each line can drift up to ~0.005 from its true share in either direction, and these independent rounding errors do not cancel out — they simply sum. Over N lines the aggregate drift can reach up to N x 0.005: e.g. six equal-weight lines splitting 0.99 each have an exact share of 0.165, which all round up to 0.17 the same way, so the six lines sum to 1.02 (3 cents invented); three equal-weight lines splitting 100.00 each have an exact share of 33.333..., which all round down to 33.33, summing to 99.99 (1 cent lost). This violates the core allocation invariant that the sum of allocated amounts must equal the total exactly.

The correct fix replaces independent per-line rounding with a technique that reconciles the sum by construction. Two standard approaches: (1) running-total / cumulative technique (BC's own VAT-rounding method): maintain a running exact (unrounded) cumulative share as you iterate lines, and set each line's Allocated Amount to Round(cumulative share so far, 0.01) minus the amount already handed out to prior lines — this guarantees the running rounded totals telescope to exactly the header total after the last line. (2) Largest-remainder method: round every line's exact share down to the cent first, sum the discarded fractional remainders to get the total shortfall in whole cents, then hand out one extra cent each to the lines with the largest discarded remainder until the sum matches the header total exactly. Either fix must also preserve that no single line drifts by a full cent or more from its exact share — dumping the entire correction onto one line (e.g. the last line) fixes the sum but can push that line's drift past the ~1-cent bound, which is itself a distinct defect. A correct diagnosis must identify that the bug is the *independence* of the per-line rounding (no shared running state / no reconciliation pass across the loop), not merely "wrong rounding function" or "off-by-one in the loop."
rows.sonnetWhy: The diagnosis matches ground truth exactly: right object (codeunit 70102, AllocateCharge second loop), right mechanic (each line's share rounded independently from the original total with no running state or reconciliation, so per-line half-cent errors sum instead of cancelling), and it reproduces both ground-truth examples (6x0.165 -> 1.02, 3x33.333 -> 99.99) while explicitly naming the independence/no-carried-remainder as the defect rather than a wrong rounding function. The fix is a legitimate reconcile-by-construction technique — a running-remainder proportional allocation (Round(RemainingAmount * Weight / RemainingWeight)) with the last weighted line taking the exact remainder — which guarantees the lines foot exactly to the header total; tracing the symptom cases, 0.99/6 yields 0.17,0.16,0.17,0.16,0.17,0.16 = 0.99 and 100.00/3 yields 33.33,33.34,33.33 = 100.00, with every line within half a cent of its exact share. It is not the disallowed dump-everything-on-the-last-line variant: the correction is redistributed progressively through the shrinking remainder, keeping per-line drift within the ~1-cent bound in the symptom scenarios and typical distributions, and it safely handles zero-weight tails and division-by-zero while leaving WeightSum, the zero-weight exit, and GetAllocatedTotal untouched.

rows.symptom: After running CalculateShipmentCosts, the "Shipment Cost" values in FIFO Shipment Cost are occasionally off by a cent from what the receiving unit costs actually add up to. It only happens on shipments that draw stock from two or more receipts (cost layers) at once, and only when the item is priced with fractional unit costs (e.g. kg or L items priced to 3-5 decimals) or the combined cost lands on an exact half-cent. Shipments that come entirely from a single layer, or whose per-layer pieces don't straddle a rounding boundary, always tie out correctly. Finance has noticed the shipment cost total for an item's outbound entries no longer reconciles exactly to the sum of what was received.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: codeunit 70052 "FIFO Costing Engine", procedure CalculateShipmentCosts, inside the inner `while Needed > 0` layer-consumption loop:
  RunningCost += Round(Take * LayerUnitCost.Get(OldestLayer), 0.01);
Each layer's dollar contribution (Take * LayerUnitCost) is rounded to the cent individually before being added into RunningCost, and RunningCost (already made of rounded pieces) is written straight to ShipmentCost."Shipment Cost" with no further rounding step. Everything else in the procedure is correct: layers are consumed strictly oldest-first via OldestLayer/LayerQty.Get/Set, a layer partially drained by one shipment correctly keeps its remainder for the next (LayerQty.Set persists the reduction), receipts posted after a shipment correctly join the back of the queue (they're only added to LayerQty/LayerUnitCost when their own ledger row is processed, later in the `repeat...until` scan), the on-hand/Insufficient-inventory guard is correct (Needed > OnHand checked before consuming any layer), and DeleteAll/Insert bookkeeping is correct.

Mechanism: summing several independently-rounded pieces is not the same number as rounding the exact (unrounded) sum once. E.g. a shipment whose two per-layer pieces are exactly 1.114 and 0.884 rounds each piece to 1.11 and 0.88 (sum 1.99), while the true combined cost 1.998 should round once to 2.00 — the stored shipment cost is a cent short. The error only appears when: (a) the shipment spans 2+ layers (a single-layer shipment rounds its one piece, which equals rounding the total — no divergence), and (b) the fractional parts of the per-layer costs straddle a rounding boundary in opposite directions (or a half-cent tie resolves differently piecewise vs. as a whole) — most random multi-layer shipments still happen to tie out, which is why the bug reads as "occasional" / cent-level noise rather than a hard failure, and why single-layer or coarsely-priced-item shipments never show it.

Correct fix: remove the Round() call from inside the while loop — accumulate RunningCost as the exact (unrounded) sum of Take * LayerUnitCost across all layers touched by the shipment — and instead round once, after the loop, when producing the stored value: ShipmentCost."Shipment Cost" := Round(RunningCost, 0.01) (equivalently, round only at the point RunningCost is assigned into the record, not per layer). No other line in the procedure needs to change. A correct diagnosis must identify specifically that rounding is being applied per-layer instead of once-per-shipment on the exact accumulated total; identifying "there's a rounding bug" or "the cost is wrong for multi-layer shipments" without naming the per-layer-vs-once-per-shipment rounding-order mechanism should be scored as partial credit at most.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver's diagnosis and fix are both the literal placeholder string "test", which identifies no object, no procedure, and no mechanism. It does not name the per-layer Round() inside the while loop in codeunit 70052 CalculateShipmentCosts, nor the round-once-per-shipment correction required by ground truth. With no root cause identified and no fix proposed, this cannot earn partial credit.
rows.fableWhy: The solver pinpointed the exact defective line (per-layer `Round(Take * LayerUnitCost, 0.01)` inside the while loop in codeunit 70052's CalculateShipmentCosts) and named the precise required mechanism: rounding each layer slice independently and summing differs from rounding the exact accumulated total once, which only diverges on multi-layer shipments whose fractional pieces straddle a rounding boundary — matching the ground truth's per-layer-vs-once-per-shipment rounding-order explanation, including why single-layer shipments always reconcile. The fix is exactly the prescribed one: accumulate RunningCost unrounded and apply `Round(RunningCost, 0.01)` once at the point the value is stored into ShipmentCost."Shipment Cost". The rest of the rewritten procedure is unchanged from correct behavior (FIFO oldest-first consumption, partial-layer remainder via LayerQty.Set, receipts appended only when scanned, the insufficient-inventory guard, DeleteAll/Insert bookkeeping, and RunningCost reset per shipment), so the fix cures the symptom without breaking anything else.

rows.symptom: Since the carrier started returning a new tracking status code, shipments carrying that status get stuck showing "Unknown" on the Shipment Tracking list, even though the carrier's own tracking portal already shows those shipments as arrived at the next stage. The existing statuses — Registered, In Transit, Delivered — still sync correctly on every refresh. Only the brand-new status the carrier introduced fails to resolve to anything but Unknown, no matter how many times the sync job is re-run.
rows.groundTruth: The defect is in Carrier Status Mapper.FromWire (codeunit 70002). It maps the incoming integer wire code to the Carrier Status enum using a hardcoded case statement with three literal branches (10 -> Registered, 20 -> In Transit, 30 -> Delivered) and an else branch that returns Unknown for anything else. Shipment Status Sync.UpdateStatus (codeunit 70003) calls FromWire for every incoming wire code and writes the result straight into Shipment Tracking.Status, so any wire code that doesn't match one of the three literal branches always lands in the else branch and is stored as Unknown — permanently, since re-running the sync executes the exact same case statement again. rows.symptom: Sales order lines don't reliably reflect the item's quality grade. Adding a fresh line for a graded item, or for a gradeless item, works fine, and switching a line from one graded item to another graded item also updates correctly. But when a line already showing a grade is re-pointed at a different item that has no grade of its own, the line keeps showing the old item's grade instead of going blank — the line no longer mirrors the item that's actually on it.
rows.groundTruth:
In LineQualityDefaults.Codeunit.al, the OnAfterAssignItemValues subscriber on "Sales Line" (procedure PullQualityGradeFromItem) wraps the copy in a guard: `if Item."Quality Grade" <> '' then SalesLine."Quality Grade" := Item."Quality Grade";`. This event fires unconditionally on every Validate("No.") for an item line, so the correct implementation is an unconditional assignment with no condition at all — the line must always mirror whatever grade the current item carries, including clearing it to blank when the item has none. The planted guard only executes the assignment when the item's grade is non-blank, so it silently no-ops when the newly-assigned item is gradeless.

Why the symptom is narrow: a brand-new line for a graded item passes (guard true, assigns correctly); a brand-new line for a gradeless item also looks correct because the field was never set in the first place, so a skipped assignment produces the same blank result as a real clear would (accidental pass, not a real one); re-validating from one graded item to another graded item passes too (guard true, overwrites). The only transition that exposes the bug is: the line currently holds a non-blank grade, and "No." is re-validated to an item whose "Quality Grade" is blank — the guard is false, the assignment is skipped, and the line is left with the stale previous grade instead of being cleared.

The fix is to delete the `if Item."Quality Grade" <> '' then` guard entirely and always execute `SalesLine."Quality Grade" := Item."Quality Grade";` unconditionally inside the subscriber, so a gradeless item explicitly overwrites the line's field with blank rather than leaving whatever value was there before.

Its explanation of why the other paths accidentally pass (fresh lines, graded-to-graded switches) mirrors the ground-truth narrow-symptom analysis. rows.symptom: Marketing builds the phone-campaign call list from a saved campaign (target city + VIP credit-limit threshold) and then iterates the resulting customer view to place calls. Customers who qualify only because they live in the campaign city are missing from the list entirely, no matter which city the campaign targets — only customers who clear the credit-limit threshold show up, including ones who happen to also live in the target city. No customer records are altered or deleted; the call list itself is just too short, silently dropping every city-only qualifier.
rows.groundTruth: Defect location: Campaign Call List.BuildCallList (CampaignCallList.Codeunit.al). The procedure runs two Mark(true) passes over the caller's Customer var-record — first SetRange(City, CampaignCity) and tag every match, then it must clear only the City filter before re-filtering on "Credit Limit (LCY)" and tagging that match too, then MarkedOnly(true) to leave the union visible. The planted bug replaces the field-scoped clear between the two passes (which should be something like Customer.SetRange(City) to drop just the City filter) with Customer.Reset(). Record.Reset() in AL clears every filter on the variable AND discards its accumulated Mark state — marks are part of the same per-variable view/filter context Reset tears down, not something that survives a filter reset. So every row tagged during the city pass is silently un-marked the instant Reset() runs, before the credit-limit pass even begins. Only rows marked during the second (credit-limit) pass survive to the final MarkedOnly(true) view. Consequence: a customer who matches ONLY the city rule ends up with no mark at all (city-pass mark wiped, and the credit-limit pass never re-tags them since their credit limit doesn't clear the threshold) — they vanish from the list. A customer who matches the credit-limit rule is unaffected regardless of city, since their mark comes entirely from the second pass which runs after the wipe. A customer matching both rules still appears (rescued by the second pass), which is why "VIP customers from the target city still show up" while "city-only customers disappear." The wrapper codeunit (Campaign Call List Mgt) and the Marketing Campaign table are not where the bug lives — they just look up campaign settings and delegate; they should be treated as correct scaffolding. Correct fix: change Customer.Reset() back to a filter clear that leaves marks untouched — e.g. Customer.SetRange(City) (or SetFilter(City, '')) to drop just the City field's filter — immediately before applying SetFilter("Credit Limit (LCY)", '>=%1', VipCreditLimit) for the second pass. General rule a correct diagnosis should state: never call Reset() on a Record variable between Mark passes whose accumulated marks must survive to the final MarkedOnly(true) — Reset clears marks along with filters, whereas SetRange/SetFilter clearing of one field does not.

Right object, right mechanic, curative fix with no collateral breakage.

rows.symptom: Our nightly exchange-rate refresh (RefreshRate in codeunit "Exchange Rate Sync", which calls "Resilient Http Client") is supposed to survive brief outages from the rates provider by retrying up to its attempt budget. In practice, whenever the provider answers with 429 (rate limited) or any 5xx status other than exactly 500 — for example 502, 503, or 504 — RefreshRate gives up after a single request and logs a failed "Integration Call Log" entry with "Total Backoff (ms)" at 0, even though several attempts were still available. The exact same kind of outage reported as a plain 500 recovers fine after one or two retries. So the rate sync's reliability depends on which specific error code the provider happens to return, not on whether the outage was actually transient.

Buggy body: `exit(StatusCode = 500)` — it treats only the literal status code 500 as retryable. Correct behavior (per the base task spec): 429 and the entire 500-599 range must all be classified transient, i.e. `exit((StatusCode = 429) or (StatusCode in [500..599]))`. Because of the narrowed check, GetWithRetry's `if not IsTransient(Response.GetHttpStatusCode()) then exit(false)` branch fires for every non-success status except exactly 500 — so 429, 501, 502, 503, 504, ... 599 are all misclassified as permanent and the call returns false after exactly one request, regardless of how large MaxAttempts is. Only a response carrying the literal integer 500 correctly loops through retries up to the attempt budget with the doubling backoff tally (BackoffDelayMs / TotalBackoffMs, which are both implemented correctly and not part of the bug). Observable mapping: "Exchange Rate Sync".RefreshRate succeeds after multiple requests when the mocked/real service returns 500 for a while then 2xx, but fails immediately (Succeeded=false, "Total Backoff (ms)"=0, exactly one HTTP request sent) when the service returns 429 or any 5xx code other than 500 — even though the same MaxAttempts budget would have recovered it exactly the way 500 does. Correct fix: replace IsTransient's condition with the full check covering 429 and the 500-599 range (as shown above). No other part of GetWithRetry, BackoffDelayMs, GetTotalBackoffMs, the call-logging table, or RefreshAllRates is defective.

rows.symptom: After the FreightEx carrier gateway went live with production traffic, every entry that Shipment Import Mgt. writes to the Shipment Import Entry log shows a Package Count of 0 and a Status of "Empty Shipment" — even for shipments that clearly aren't empty. The same log row's Tracking No. Count and Weight Unit columns come back populated and correct, so packages obviously did arrive; only the package count is wrong. GetLastImportedPackageCount likewise always reports 0 for any shipment. Nothing throws an error anywhere — the import just runs and silently under-counts every single time, whereas it worked fine against the old sandbox test messages.
rows.groundTruth: Defect location: codeunit "Shipment Status Parser" (70101), procedure CountPackages. It calls Doc.SelectNodes('//Package', NsManager, PackageNodes) — the XPath step "Package" has no namespace prefix. Mechanism: production ShipmentStatus messages put every shipping-namespace element (ShipmentStatus, Header, ShipmentNo, Packages, Package, Weight) into the namespace urn:tryal:freight:shipping:v2, either via a default xmlns="..." declaration on the root or via an explicit prefix — the FreightEx spec allows either, and prefixes are the sender's free choice. In XPath, an UNPREFIXED element name always means "this element in NO namespace," never "whatever the default namespace happens to be." So '//Package' matches zero nodes on any spec-conformant message, regardless of whether the sender used a default declaration or a prefix, because Package is never actually in no namespace. This is why the code "works" only on old unnamespaced sandbox samples and silently returns 0 in production. Why the rest of the app still works: the same LoadWithNamespaces helper builds one correctly-configured XmlNamespaceManager (NsManager.NameTable(Doc.NameTable()) + AddNamespace('sh', ShippingNsLbl) + AddNamespace('trk', TrackingNsLbl)) and CountPackages receives and passes that same NsManager into SelectNodes — the manager itself is fine and available. GetShipmentNo ('/sh:ShipmentStatus/sh:Header/sh:ShipmentNo'), GetTrackingNumbers ('//trk:TrackingNo'), and GetWeightUnit ('//sh:Weight/@unit') all correctly prefix every element step with the bound sh:/trk: aliases, so they resolve correctly against both default-namespace and prefixed-namespace documents — only the one query in CountPackages omits its prefix. That asymmetry (GetTrackingNumbers finding real tracking numbers, proving packages exist, while CountPackages simultaneously reports 0) is the diagnostic tell that should point a correct diagnosis at CountPackages specifically rather than at the namespace manager setup, the table, or Shipment Import Mgt.'s orchestration logic (which is a faithful, correct consumer of whatever CountPackages returns). Correct fix: change the XPath literal in CountPackages from '//Package' to '//sh:Package', matching the prefixing pattern already used correctly everywhere else in the codeunit, so the query resolves through the 'sh' alias bound to the shipping namespace URI and counts every shipping-namespace Package element regardless of how the sender declared that namespace.

rows.symptom: The customer search box is supposed to return a hit whenever the typed text appears in a customer's Name or its City, but Customer Search Service.Search (and SearchContactable) is only counting customers where the text shows up in BOTH the name and the city at once. A customer whose name matches the term but whose city doesn't (or vice versa) never shows up in the count, so the totals users see are consistently too low, sometimes zero for a search that should clearly find someone. The Customer Search Log entries the service writes faithfully record whatever number Search computed, so the log itself isn't wrong - the count it's logging is just already too small. Support has described it as "the customer search only finds someone if the name and the city both match the word."
rows.groundTruth: Defect location: Customer Cross Search (codeunit 70000), local procedure ApplyCrossColumnSearch, called by both CountMatches and CountContactableMatches (and transitively by Customer Search Service's Search/SearchContactable in codeunit 70001). The procedure calls Customer.SetFilter(Name, '@*'+SearchText+'*') and Customer.SetFilter(City, '@*'+SearchText+'*') back to back without ever changing the record's filter group - both filters land in the default filter group (group 0). In AL, all filters set within the same filter group are ANDed together: a record must satisfy every filter in that group to be returned. So the current code requires a customer to match the search text in Name AND City simultaneously (an intersection), even though each individual @*text* wildcard filter is syntactically and semantically correct on its own - the bug is not in the filter syntax, it's in which filter group the two filters share. After that fix, a customer matching in Name only, City only, or both counts exactly once (never twice), and the "contactable" narrowing only ever removes customers from that union, never adds one on e-mail alone. A correct diagnosis must name FilterGroup(-1)/the OR-vs-AND filter-group semantics as the missing piece, not just "the two filters need to be combined with OR" in the abstract - restoring FilterGroup(0) afterward is also required, since leaving the record parked in group -1 would silently fold any later added filter (like the e-mail check) into the OR set instead of narrowing the union.

rows.symptom: Correcting a mis-typed provisioning batch number (via "Provisioning Batch Correction") gets noticeably slower than it should as the batch grows: renumbering a batch of a few hundred slots costs roughly double the database work you'd expect for that many rows. The operation still completes and every slot ends up correctly moved to the new batch number with all its Label, External Ref, and Notes intact - nothing is wrong with the result, only with how much work it takes to produce it. The slowdown scales with the number of slots in the batch, not with the total size of the table.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: ProvisioningSlotMgt.Codeunit.al, procedure RenumberBatch(OldBatchNo, NewBatchNo: Code[20]).

Mechanic: The procedure calls ProvisioningSlot.SetLoadFields("Batch No.", "Slot No.") before FindSet/repeat, narrowing the loaded column set to just the two primary-key fields, then calls ProvisioningSlot.Rename(NewBatchNo, ProvisioningSlot."Slot No.") on each row in the loop. Rename physically deletes the row under its old primary key and re-inserts it under the new key, which requires the full record (all columns: Label, External Ref, Notes, Provisioned At) to write back - not just the key fields. Because SetLoadFields only cached the key columns, the platform must issue an implicit JIT (just-in-time) reload of the missing columns for every single row before Rename can execute. The net effect is 2 SQL statements per row (1 for the JIT reload + 1 for the rename/write) instead of the 1 statement per row a plain, unnarrowed Get/FindSet + Rename would cost - the SetLoadFields call does not save a statement here, it adds one, because the very next operation on each record (Rename) needs everything SetLoadFields excluded.

Why the symptom follows: for a batch of N slots, the naive code costs roughly 2N SQL statements (measurable via SessionInformation.SqlStatementsExecuted); the correct code costs roughly N. The overhead scales linearly with batch size, matching "the slowdown scales with the number of slots," and produces a correct final result (Rename still succeeds and all fields survive), matching "nothing is wrong with the result, only with how much work it takes."

Correct fix: remove the SetLoadFields("Batch No.", "Slot No.") call entirely (let FindSet load the full record as normal), since narrowing the columns buys nothing when every row is about to be renamed and rename needs the whole row anyway. (Equivalently, a fix could call SetLoadFields with every field the table has, but that is pointless indirection versus simply not narrowing at all.) A judge should credit any diagnosis that identifies: (1) the SetLoadFields call in RenumberBatch as the root cause, (2) that Rename requires the full record and forces a JIT reload of the excluded columns, and (3) that removing/loosening the SetLoadFields call is the fix. A diagnosis that only says "add SetLoadFields is good practice, so no bug here" or blames CreateSlot/CountSlots/CorrectBatchNo (which are correct) should NOT be credited.

rows.symptom: Entering or pasting applied entries into the search grid gets progressively slower the further into a session the user is - the first few rows feel instant, but by the time a hundred rows have been entered each new row visibly hangs before its running total updates. Sessions that paste in a large batch of rows can take minutes where a handful of rows takes a fraction of a second, even though every row carries the same amount of data. Deleting an already-applied row and re-adding it does not fix the slowdown; it reappears and keeps compounding as more rows are entered. No error ever appears - it is purely a growing wait.
rows.groundTruth: Defect is in codeunit 70003 "CG Applied Total Mgt", procedure AddAppliedEntry. The codeunit keeps a running list of every entry number added so far in the session (the global KnownEntryNo list). On EVERY call - i.e. once per row the user enters or pastes - the procedure clears the entire "CG Applied Total Buffer" temporary table (Buffer.DeleteAll) and then rebuilds it from scratch by looping over the FULL KnownEntryNo list, doing one LedgerEntry.Get() plus one LedgerEntry.CalcFields("Remaining Amount") - a SIFT sum over child table "CG Applied Entry Detail" - for every entry number ever added, not just the newly added one. So the Nth call re-fetches and re-aggregates all N entries (the N-1 whose Remaining Amount was already correctly buffered, plus the 1 new one), instead of only touching the new entry and leaving the previously-computed buffer rows untouched. Each Get/CalcFields pair targets a structurally distinct ledger entry (different EntryNo key each call), so nothing is absorbed by record-cache reuse - the cost is real, additive database round trips. Across a session of M sequential AddAppliedEntry calls, total round trips sum to 1+2+...+M = O(M^2), which is exactly why per-row latency grows with session length and total session time grows quadratically rather than linearly. RemoveAppliedEntry is NOT defective - it updates the list and deletes the single buffer row directly, O(1) - so a correct diagnosis should isolate the clear-and-full-rebuild pattern specifically inside AddAppliedEntry, not accuse the buffer table, the FlowField/CalcFormula definition, or RemoveAppliedEntry. The correct fix: AddAppliedEntry should perform Get()+CalcFields() ONLY for NewEntryNo, then Insert (or Modify, if the entry number recurs) just that single Buffer row - leaving every previously-inserted Buffer row exactly as it is, since a given entry's Remaining Amount was already computed correctly and does not change by virtue of a different entry being added. That reduces the routine to O(1) database round trips per call and O(M) total across a full M-row session, with GetBufferTotal's linear scan over the buffer unchanged.

rows.symptom: Before closing an accounting period, we call the check that tells us whether any Annual or Quarterly reference reports are still outstanding as of the period-end date (HasPendingReferenceUpToPeriodEnd). This used to return almost instantly, but it has gotten progressively slower as the number of entries in the outbound reference queue has grown, even in periods where the true answer is "nothing outstanding" and at most one queue entry is actually overdue. The slowdown tracks the total size of the queue, not how many reports are genuinely pending as of the cutoff date.
rows.groundTruth: Defect lives in codeunit 70000 "CG Reference Process", procedure HasPendingReferenceUpToPeriodEnd(PeriodEndingDate: Date). It filters table 70000 "CG Outbound Queue Entry" only by Report Type (SetFilter "Report Type", Annual|Quarterly) - there is no date filter and no stored date column on the queue table itself, only a "Source Record Id" (Guid) pointing at the SystemId of a row in table 70001 "CG Member Report Source", which holds the real "Posting Date". FindSet then walks every matching queue row and, per row, calls the local helper GetDocumentDate(SourceRecordId), which opens a RecordRef on "CG Member Report Source" (RecRef.Open(Database::"CG Member Report Source")) and calls RecRef.GetBySystemId(SourceRecordId) - one extra full database round-trip/point lookup per queue row - purely to read that row's Posting Date and compare it to PeriodEndingDate. The loop exits(true) as soon as it finds a qualifying row (DocumentDate <> 0D and <= PeriodEndingDate), so a queue where the overdue entry happens to sort early can return fast; the pathological, common case is "nothing is actually due", where the function must scan and GetBySystemId every single matching queue row before it can return false. Because the queue table carries no date of its own, this cross-table point-lookup cost is unavoidable in the current design and is O(N) in the number of matching queue rows regardless of how many are truly overdue - e.g. a 500-row queue with only 1 genuinely-due document costs roughly 500 extra SQL round-trips via GetBySystemId versus the ~1 a date-aware design would need. Correct fix: denormalize the source document's date onto "CG Outbound Queue Entry" itself (add a Posting Date / Reference Date field, populated once in EnqueueReference from Source."Posting Date" at enqueue time), then rewrite HasPendingReferenceUpToPeriodEnd as a single filtered existence check - SetFilter("Report Type", ...), SetFilter(<new date field>, '<=%1', PeriodEndingDate), IsEmpty() (negated) or FindFirst - eliminating the per-row RecordRef/GetBySystemId call entirely so the check costs O(1) SQL statements independent of queue size. A fix that only adds SetLoadFields to the existing FindSet, or reorders the loop, does not resolve the defect: the per-row cross-table GetBySystemId call is the expensive operation, and it fires once per matching queue row regardless of which fields are loaded on the queue record itself.
