This eliminates the per-row cross-table lookup (not a SetLoadFields band-aid) and returns the same boolean, so it cures the symptom without breaking other behavior.

rows.symptom: After running the loyalty program's priority-support eligibility check, several customers who have clearly crossed the 5,000 lifetime-spend threshold are left with "Priority Support Approved" unchecked, while other customers with similar or even lower spend do get approved. On the unapproved customers, "Manual VIP Override" shows No, and turning it on does get them approved, but customers are supposed to also qualify on spend alone and right now some legitimately high-spending customers don't. The pattern is inconsistent run to run and doesn't line up with the spend amount at all, which points at the check itself being unreliable rather than the 5,000 threshold being set wrong.
rows.groundTruth: Location: codeunit 70001 "CG Loyalty Gatekeeper", procedure EvaluateCandidate, publishes local IntegrationEvent OnCheckPriorityEligibility(Candidate; var Eligible: Boolean) with Eligible initialized false; subscribers are meant to only ADD to it (an additive/monotonic contract that is implied by the shared var but never enforced by the platform). Codeunit 70002 "CG Loyalty Rule Spend" subscribes correctly and additively: `if Candidate."Lifetime Spend" >= 5000 then Eligible := true;` (never turns Eligible back off). Codeunit 70003 "CG Loyalty Rule VIP" is the planted defect: it subscribes with an UNCONDITIONAL assignment, `Eligible := Candidate."Manual VIP Override";`, instead of the monotonic form `if Candidate."Manual VIP Override" then Eligible := true;`. Business Central does not guarantee the bind/execution order of multiple subscribers on the same event. When "CG Loyalty Rule VIP" happens to run AFTER "CG Loyalty Rule Spend" for a candidate whose Lifetime Spend >= 5000 but whose Manual VIP Override = false, the VIP rule's unconditional Eligible := false silently erases the Spend rule's correct Eligible := true, and EvaluateCandidate then persists Priority Support Approved := false for a customer who should have qualified on spend alone. The fault is order-dependent/nondeterministic, not a threshold, rounding, filter, or data-persistence bug: the same candidate can get a different outcome across runs, and two candidates with identical Lifetime Spend can diverge purely based on whether the VIP subscriber happened to run last. Correct fix: make the VIP subscriber additive/monotonic like the Spend subscriber (only ever set Eligible := true, never assign it a plain boolean that can be false), so no subscriber can clear a true already set by another; a more robust fix gives each subscriber its own out-parameter/reason and has the publisher combine them with OR so the result is order-independent by construction. A diagnosis that blames the 5,000 threshold value, "Lifetime Spend" data/rounding, the SetRange/FindSet filter in EvaluateAllPending, or a missing Commit/Modify does not identify the actual defect.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified exactly the planted defect: codeunit 70003 "CG Loyalty Rule VIP"'s subscriber performing an unconditional `Eligible := Candidate."Manual VIP Override";` that clobbers the Spend rule's `true` whenever the platform happens to invoke the VIP subscriber after the Spend subscriber, correctly citing AL's unguaranteed subscriber execution order as the source of the run-to-run nondeterminism. This matches the ground truth's object, mechanic, and explanation of the symptom (spend-independent, inconsistent, VIP-on masking the bug) point for point, and it does not blame any of the decoy causes (threshold, rounding, filters, Commit/Modify). The proposed fix, `if Candidate."Manual VIP Override" then Eligible := true;`, is precisely the monotonic/additive correction the ground truth names as the correct fix, cures the symptom by making the outcome an order-independent OR, and preserves the VIP-override path without touching any other code.

rows.symptom: We renamed a product category (for example from an old code to a new one), and every product under that category correctly shows the new category code afterward - opening any product confirms it. But the saved report filter that was set up to summarize that category's products (created via the report-filter setup, queried through the "matching products" count) now returns zero products, even though the same products are still assigned to the category and nothing else about the filter was touched. The filter's own stored category code still shows the OLD code, as if the category rename never reached it, while every product record was updated as expected.
rows.groundTruth: Codeunit "Category Rename Mgt." (id 70200), procedure RenameCategory(OldCode, NewCode): it calls ProductCategory.Rename(NewCode) on the primary key of table "Product Category" (70200), then calls the local UpdateProductAssignments helper, which correctly walks every "Product" (70201) row where Category Code = OldCode and rewrites it to NewCode - Product.Category Code carries a proper TableRelation to Product Category.Code, and this sibling is fully cascaded. Table "Category Report Filter" (70202) also stores a Category Code value, but as a PLAIN Code[20] field with no TableRelation - just a value copied in at insert time via CreateReportFilter. RenameCategory never visits Category Report Filter at all, so after a rename every filter row for that category is left holding the OLD code while every actual Product row now holds the NEW code. CountMatchingProducts(FilterCode) does CategoryReportFilter.Get(FilterCode) then Product.SetRange("Category Code", CategoryReportFilter."Category Code") - it filters by the STALE old code, which no Product carries anymore, so it returns 0 even though the data is entirely self-consistent on the Product side. This is candidate #2 from docs/reasoning-suite/sweeps/sweep-b2-postgres-logic.md ("Rename doesn't cascade to a sibling table's plain-copied key field"): only one of two sibling tables that copy the parent key gets fixed up on rename; the plain-value copy in the second table is invisible to Rename() because nothing at the platform level (no TableRelation, no trigger) ties it back to the parent, and there is no compile-time or runtime signal exposing the gap. A correct fix makes RenameCategory also update every Category Report Filter row whose Category Code equals OldCode to NewCode (e.g. an additional SetRange/FindSet/Modify loop over Category Report Filter parallel to UpdateProductAssignments, or a shared cascade helper invoked for every table that copies the key by value), so the filter's stored code stays in sync with the category's live code after any rename.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver's diagnosis matches ground truth exactly: it names codeunit 70200 "Category Rename Mgt."/RenameCategory, identifies the missing cascade to table 70202 "Category Report Filter" (whose plain-copied Category Code is never rewritten while UpdateProductAssignments fixes up Product), and correctly traces the symptom through CountMatchingProducts filtering Product by the stale OldCode, yielding 0. The proposed fix adds an UpdateReportFilterAssignments loop (SetRange on OldCode, FindSet, rewrite to NewCode, Modify) parallel to the existing Product cascade and invoked from RenameCategory — precisely the fix the ground truth prescribes, curing the symptom without touching CreateReportFilter, CountMatchingProducts, or other behavior. The only quibble is a platform-lore aside claiming TableRelation fields are never auto-cascaded on Rename, but this does not alter the correctly identified object, mechanic, or the validity of the fix.

rows.symptom: Running Reissue on a batch whose Reissue Setup is not fully configured leaves the system with NO batch header at all for that batch number — where before the call there was at least the old one. Users report that a batch they were trying to refresh simply vanishes: it isn't replaced with a new one, and re-running Reissue afterward doesn't recreate it either (Default Batch Template is still blank, so it keeps failing the same way). The old batch's Description, Template Code and Created Date are all gone with it.
rows.groundTruth: Defect location: codeunit "Batch Reissue Mgt." (70002), procedure Reissue(BatchNo). Mechanic: Reissue filters Batch Header to the given No., calls DeleteAll(true), and then calls Commit() BEFORE calling the local procedure BuildReplacementBatch(BatchNo) that creates the new header. BuildReplacementBatch does ReissueSetup.Get() followed by ReissueSetup.TestField("Default Batch Template") — if the single Reissue Setup record is missing, or exists but has a blank Default Batch Template, TestField (or Get) raises a runtime error. Because Commit() was already called after DeleteAll, the deletion of the old Batch Header row is permanently persisted to the database and cannot be rolled back by the ensuing error — AL only auto-rolls-back the current (uncommitted) transaction, and the delete is no longer part of it. The insert of NewBatchHeader in BuildReplacementBatch never happens because the error is thrown before Insert(true) is reached. Net effect: the old batch header is gone, no new one was created, and the caller sees a runtime error that gives no indication a destructive write already survived it — a diagnosing model would need to recognize that the Commit() between DeleteAll and the fallible BuildReplacementBatch step is what makes the deletion durable independent of the later failure. Correct fix: remove the Commit() call (or restructure so DeleteAll and the new Insert happen atomically in one transaction, e.g. validate/TestField the setup BEFORE deleting the old header, or wrap both delete and insert without an intervening Commit so a later failure rolls back the delete too). A judge should credit a diagnosis that identifies (a) the Commit() call sitting between the DeleteAll and the setup-validation/insert step as the root cause, (b) that this makes the old-batch deletion irreversible regardless of what happens afterward, and (c) that the observable symptom (batch disappears with no replacement) follows because the code that would create the replacement fails AFTER the point of no return. A diagnosis that only blames "TestField throwing" or "missing setup data" without identifying the premature Commit as what makes the deletion unrecoverable should NOT be credited as fully correct.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified exactly the planted mechanic: the Commit() in codeunit 70002 "Batch Reissue Mgt." sitting between DeleteAll(true) and the fallible BuildReplacementBatch (ReissueSetup.Get + TestField), and explicitly explained that the commit makes the deletion durable so the subsequent TestField error cannot roll it back — satisfying all three credit criteria (a), (b), and (c) in the ground truth, not merely blaming TestField or missing setup. The fix removes the mid-procedure Commit() and additionally moves Get/TestField validation before the delete, which is precisely one of the correct fixes the ground truth names; the happy path (delete then insert from template, same fields, Status::Open, Insert(true)) is preserved as one atomic transaction, and the signature change to the local BuildReplacementBatch is internal-only, so no other behavior breaks.

rows.symptom: When two external contacts get merged upstream so that one contact's feed identifier now matches another contact already in our system, the losing contact keeps receiving updates from the feed (company name, VAT registration no., address, status, last-synced timestamp all keep refreshing) but its Contact Id in our system never changes to the merged/target id. The two contacts stay permanently split under different ids even though the feed has been reporting them as one identity for a long time, and no error or warning is ever raised about the conflict.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: codeunit "Contact Sync" (ContactSync.Codeunit.al), local procedure RenameContact, called from procedure SyncContact.

Mechanic: RenameContact(var Contact; NewContactId) checks `if OtherContact.Get(NewContactId) then exit;` — when the target id is already taken by another "External Contact" row, it returns with no error, no return value, and no signal of any kind ("if Target.Get(...) then exit" idiom reads as an ordinary no-op guard). Its caller, SyncContact, has no way to distinguish "rename succeeded" from "rename was skipped due to a collision": after calling RenameContact it unconditionally proceeds to overwrite Company Name, VAT Registration No., Address, Status, and Last Synced on the Contact record and calls Contact.Modify(true) — against the record which, on the collision path, is STILL keyed under its OLD Contact Id (Rename() was never actually called, so the record's primary key never changed).

Why the symptom follows: on every subsequent sync of that same feed row (same LocalContactId, same colliding target NewContactId), the same sequence repeats — Get the old-keyed row, attempt-and-silently-skip the rename, then blindly refresh and Modify() every other field. The row's identity field is permanently and silently stuck at the old value while every other field keeps being refreshed forever, exactly matching "other fields keep updating from the feed forever, but its id in our system never changes to match."

Correct fix: RenameContact must communicate the collision outcome to its caller (e.g. return a Boolean success/failure, or raise an error) instead of a bare `exit`. SyncContact must then branch on that result — on a collision it should NOT proceed to call Modify() on the stale-keyed record (or must otherwise flag/skip the update and surface the conflict), rather than unconditionally refreshing and saving the other fields regardless of whether the rename actually happened. A judge should credit any diagnosis that identifies: (1) the `if OtherContact.Get(NewContactId) then exit;` early-return with no return value/error as the root cause, (2) that the caller cannot tell rename-succeeded apart from rename-skipped-on-collision, and (3) that the caller's unconditional Contact.Modify(true) after the rename attempt is what causes the other fields to keep updating on a still-wrong-keyed row.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified exactly the planted mechanic: the `if OtherContact.Get(NewContactId) then exit;` bare early-return in RenameContact, the caller's inability to distinguish rename-succeeded from rename-skipped, and SyncContact's unconditional field refresh plus Contact.Modify(true) on the still-old-keyed record, matching all three credit criteria in the ground truth. The proposed fix raises a descriptive Error on the collision path, which is one of the two remediation options the ground truth explicitly sanctions ("return a Boolean ... or raise an error"), and it prevents the caller from reaching the Modify block while surfacing the conflict to the operator. The success path (no collision, first-time insert) is preserved since Get still returns false there and Rename executes as before. This is a correct root-cause diagnosis with a fix that cures the symptom without altering non-collision behavior.

rows.symptom: Running the "Copy Document" action on a document sometimes fails outright with a database error saying the record has been changed and needs to be reopened, while other times the exact same action completes without any error. When it does fail, the new document has already been created with its Status showing Released, but the "Copy Audited" flag on that document never gets set — the audit step silently gets skipped rather than raising anything the user would notice, unless the whole action also throws the version-conflict error and the copy appears to fail even though the document row already exists.
rows.groundTruth:
Codeunit 70001 "CG Document Copy Mgt", procedure CopyDocument, inserts the new "CG Document Header" row and raises the local integration event OnAfterCopyDocument(var DocHeader), threading that one shared record-variable reference through to every subscriber in the invocation chain.

Subscriber Codeunit 70002 "CG Copy Status Mgt" (procedure AutoReleaseCopiedDocument) does NOT write through the DocHeader parameter it was handed. It opens a SEPARATE record instance via DocumentHeader.Get(DocHeader."No."), sets Status := Released, and calls Modify(true) on that separate instance. This is a legitimate write, but because it commits through a distinct in-memory record variable, it bumps the row's version/timestamp in the database out from under the publisher's original DocHeader instance.

Subscriber Codeunit 70003 "CG Copy Audit Mgt" (procedure MarkDocumentAudited) receives the SAME shared DocHeader parameter passed down from the publisher — still holding the pre-70002-write row version, because it was never re-fetched after 70002's independent commit — sets "Copy Audited" := true, and calls DocHeader.Modify(false) directly on it.

The defect: Modify(false) only suppresses the record's OnModify trigger; it does NOT bypass Business Central's optimistic-concurrency row-version check on the underlying SQL UPDATE. Because subscriber 70002 already advanced the row's version through its own separate Get()'d instance, subscriber 70003's Modify(false) call on the now-stale DocHeader collides with that version and throws BC's "This record has been changed by another user" / not-up-to-date runtime error. This aborts the "Copy Audited" write (and, depending on how the caller surfaces subscriber errors, can make the whole CopyDocument call appear to fail) even though Status was correctly set to Released moments earlier by subscriber 70002.

Whether the failure actually manifests depends entirely on subscriber execution order and on whether both subscribers are active: if 70002 had not yet run when 70003 executed, or if only one subscriber were bound, no version conflict would occur — which is exactly why the symptom is intermittent ("sometimes fails, sometimes doesn't") rather than a deterministic crash.

Correct fix: subscriber 70003 (or any subscriber that runs after another subscriber has independently written the same row through its own separate record instance) must re-fetch the row immediately before writing — i.e. call DocHeader.Get(DocHeader."No.") to refresh its version/timestamp — before setting "Copy Audited" and calling Modify, rather than trusting that the var parameter it was handed at subscription time still reflects the current database state. Merely changing Modify(false) to Modify(true) does NOT fix the bug, since the RunTrigger argument has no bearing on the optimistic-concurrency version check; the required fix is the missing Get()/re-read before the second Modify.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver identified the exact planted defect: codeunit 70003's MarkDocumentAudited writes through the stale shared var DocHeader (frozen at post-Insert state) while sibling subscriber 70002 independently commits Status=Released through its own Get()'d instance, advancing the row version and making 70003's Modify collide with BC's optimistic-concurrency check. It correctly states the key mechanic that Modify(false) only suppresses the OnModify trigger and does not bypass the version check, and correctly attributes the intermittency to unguaranteed subscriber ordering. The proposed fix (re-fetch the row via Get on the "No." before setting "Copy Audited" and calling Modify, mirroring 70002's pattern) is exactly the ground-truth remedy; using a fresh local record variable rather than refreshing the var parameter is functionally equivalent, cures both faces of the symptom, and leaves signatures, bindings, and other behavior untouched.

rows.symptom: The "Some search rules are incomplete" notification appears on every single page open, even when every rule in the list is already marked complete. It never goes away no matter how many rules the user finishes. Turning off "Advanced Filtering Enabled" in the Search Setup is supposed to disable the automatic incomplete-rule check entirely, but instead it seems to make the notification fire even more aggressively - it now shows up as soon as there is any rule at all in the system, complete or not.
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: codeunit "CG Search Rule Mgt" (id 70000), procedure FilterIncompleteRules(var SearchRule: Record "CG Search Rule"). When the CG Search Setup record does not exist (SearchSetup.Get() fails) or "Advanced Filtering Enabled" is false, the procedure does a bare `exit;` and returns without applying ANY filter to the SearchRule var-record parameter - it never applies `SearchRule.SetRange(Completed, false)` in that branch. The correct behavior for "filtering is off" should be to filter to zero rows (e.g. SearchRule.SetRange("Entry No.", 0), or some other empty-result filter), not to leave the record completely unfiltered.

Why the symptom follows: the caller, ShowIncompleteRulesNotification(), calls FilterIncompleteRules(SearchRule) and then tests `if not SearchRule.IsEmpty() then <send notification>`. When the flag branch exits early, SearchRule carries no filter at all, so IsEmpty() is checking "does the CG Search Rule table contain ANY row whatsoever" rather than "does it contain any incomplete row." That is true the moment a single rule of any completion state exists, so the notification fires unconditionally/on every page open regardless of whether rules are actually incomplete - and paradoxically fires MORE often with advanced filtering disabled (unfiltered = matches everything) than with it enabled (filtered to Completed = false, which correctly returns empty once all rules are done).

The bug is a guard-clause/early-exit control-flow defect, not a syntax error: the code compiles and runs; `exit` with no return value is valid for a procedure with a var-parameter output style. The caller cannot distinguish "the callee decided not to filter" from "the callee filtered to nothing," so it silently inherits the callee's no-op as if it were a real filtering decision.

Correct fix: either (a) inside FilterIncompleteRules, when the flag is off, apply a filter that yields zero matching rows (e.g. SearchRule.SetRange("Entry No.", 0) or an equivalent always-false filter) instead of a bare exit, so IsEmpty() correctly reports "no incomplete rules" in that state; or (b) restructure the contract so the caller only checks IsEmpty() when FilterIncompleteRules explicitly signals that filtering was applied (e.g. return a Boolean "FilterApplied" and skip the notification entirely when it's false). Either fix must preserve the case where SearchRule.SetRange(Completed, false) legitimately runs and returns real incomplete rows.

A grader should mark a diagnosis correct if it identifies: (1) FilterIncompleteRules's early exit leaves the Record var-parameter with no filter applied in the flag-off/no-setup path, (2) the caller's IsEmpty() check on that unfiltered record matches any row in the table rather than only incomplete ones, and (3) the fix must make the "filtering disabled" path produce an empty result set (or otherwise suppress the IsEmpty() check), not merely "add a filter somewhere" or "fix the notification text."
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver's diagnosis matches ground truth on all three required points: it pinpoints FilterIncompleteRules' bare early exit leaving the var-record parameter unfiltered in the no-setup/flag-off branches, explains that ShowIncompleteRulesNotification's IsEmpty() then tests "any row exists" instead of "any incomplete row exists," and correctly derives the paradoxical fires-more-with-flag-off behavior (unfiltered superset vs. Completed=false subset). The proposed fix is ground truth's sanctioned option (b): restructure so the caller gates on the setup record and flag and only evaluates IsEmpty() after explicitly applying SetRange(Completed, false), suppressing the notification entirely when filtering is disabled, while preserving the legitimate incomplete-rules path. Leaving FilterIncompleteRules untouched is a deliberate, explained contract choice (other callers may want the unfiltered list), not a dodge, and the fix cures the symptom without breaking MarkRuleComplete/CreateRule or other behavior.

rows.symptom: Opening a brand-new, unsaved Expense Report and clicking into its Comments subform hangs the client for a long time before showing a count. The number it finally shows is not 0 (which is correct for a report that has no comments yet) — it's some large, unrelated total, and it changes depending on how many other people's in-progress expense reports currently sit unsaved in the system. Users report it "feels like it's counting every comment in the company, not just this report's."
rows.groundTruth:
Defect location: CGExpenseCommentMgt.Codeunit.al, procedure CountRelatedComments (invoked from CGExpenseReportComments.Page.al's OnFindRecord trigger, which fires every time the comments ListPart repositions — including immediately when a brand-new, not-yet-inserted Expense Report's subform opens).

Mechanic: the procedure derives the "current report" key by calling CommentLineRec.GetFilter("Expense Report No.") and Evaluate-ing the result into ReportNo, then guards with `if ReportNo = '' then` to short-circuit for a record with no key. This assumes GetFilter() returns a true empty string when the field's filter is blank/unset. It does not: Business Central's GetFilter() returns a two-character sentinel token for "field value is blank" filter syntax, not literal empty string, whenever the underlying field is blank (as it is on a brand-new, unsaved record). Evaluate() succeeds and assigns that sentinel text into ReportNo, so `ReportNo = ''` is false and the intended early-exit never fires.

Execution falls through to `OtherCommentLine.SetFilter("Expense Report No.", ReportNo)`. Because SetFilter (unlike SetRange) interprets its argument AS filter syntax rather than a literal value, and the sentinel text IS valid BC filter syntax for "field is blank," this line accidentally becomes a syntactically well-formed filter that matches every CG Expense Comment Line row across every expense report whose "Expense Report No." is itself blank — i.e., every other user's unsaved/in-progress report's orphaned comment lines, company-wide — instead of matching nothing (the correct behavior for a report with no key yet). CommentCount is then set to that company-wide row count, and because SetFilter+Count on an unrestricted/no-key scope can touch a large number of rows, the UI stalls while it evaluates.

Why the symptom follows: any brand-new report shares the same blank key, so this bug is invisible on a saved report (which has a real "No." with a real filter) and only manifests on unsaved records — matching "opening a brand-new, unsaved report" in the symptom. The count shown has nothing to do with the current report; it's the count of blank-keyed comment lines system-wide, which grows over time as more users leave reports unsaved.

Correct fix: don't derive the key via GetFilter()/Evaluate() at all — read the record's own field value directly (CommentLineRec."Expense Report No.") for the comparison and the subsequent SetFilter/SetRange call. If GetFilter() must be used (e.g. because the true intent is to inspect an explicit filter rather than the field value), the blank/unset case must be detected some way OTHER than comparing the returned text to a literal empty string — e.g. checking whether a filter is actually applied via a filter-group/FilterIsChanged style check, or simply not calling SetFilter at all when no meaningful key exists. Note codeunit procedure UpdateReportSummary in the same file shows the correct pattern already (SetRange off the record's actual field, not a filter string), which is why a saved report's own summary count is unaffected — only the subform's live OnFindRecord count (CountRelatedComments) carries the defect.
rows.sonnetWhy: The solver named the exact defect site (CountRelatedComments in the CG Expense Comment Mgt. codeunit) and the exact mechanic: GetFilter("Expense Report No.") returns the two-character blank-value sentinel rather than a true empty string, Evaluate copies it verbatim so the `ReportNo = ''` guard never fires, and the fall-through SetFilter reinterprets that sentinel as filter syntax for "field is blank," counting every blank-keyed comment line company-wide — matching ground truth point for point, including why the number tracks other users' unsaved reports and why the count is slow. The proposed fix is exactly the ground-truth remedy: read CommentLineRec."Expense Report No." directly (the same pattern UpdateReportSummary already uses) and switch to SetRange, which makes the blank guard fire correctly for unsaved records while leaving saved-report counts unchanged. Nothing in the fix breaks other behavior.
